Transcribes the six original battle tables out of the retail cartridge. Takes the ROM path from --rom or YDIJ_ROM and hard-codes no drive letter, so CI never needs the cartridge; verifies the ROM SHA-256 and the DIGIMONCHAMP/YDIJ header, derives the ARM9 ROM offset and RAM base from the header rather than assuming 0x4000, and refuses to write any table whose record count does not converge against a boundary in the image.

596 move records, stride 104, from ARM9 0x020CFF9C. Eight named fields; 36 more carry a traced read site and keep their byte offset as their name. The 596 Japanese names stay in the cartridge -- only the name pointer is transcribed.
11 arena records, stride 24, from ARM9 0x020CC148. Five ASCII asset-token pointers and one u32; the identifier column is BATTLE_NORMAL through BATTLE_DOMESTADIUM.
46 records, stride 40, from ARM9 0x020CC8D4 -- a corrected base and a corrected count; see correctionForSharedLedger.
62 records, stride 40, from ARM9 0x020CD004. Record 61 is the only one whose +0x24 is zero, which is the OVL8 no-reward special case pinned from data.
152 records, stride 20, from ARM9 0x020ED2D8 -- a corrected base; see correctionForSharedLedger.
456 records, stride 68, from ARM9 0x020E39D8. The count is cross-checked by the opponent-team table, whose three index columns name exactly 0..455.

Read-only accessor over the six catalogs: record counts, the ARM9 base/stride layout, a field reader that covers fields declared once as a table constant, and the species move scan with the eight-record cap from OVL19 0x02113DC0. Imports nothing outside src. Nothing else imports it -- B1 is data, not wiring.

17 cases. Ten hand-checked records carry their original bytes as hex and are decoded independently of the builder, so a wrong base, width or stride fails here. Also pins each record count and its convergence, the two base corrections, the enum ranges their dispatch code allows, the arena token list, the 0..455 preset bijection, that no catalog file contains a non-ASCII byte or an escaped one, and that no field is named unless a read site supports it.

Transcribes the 52-entry dispatch table and OVL19's script blob. Takes the ROM path from --rom or YDIJ_ROM and hard-codes no drive letter; verifies the cartridge SHA-256, refuses to emit unless the table ends on the stack-overflow assert strings and a linear decode of the blob closes exactly on the byte where ARM code resumes with every branch target on an instruction boundary.
The opcode table with per-opcode occurrence counts, the 63,748-byte bytecode blob as base64, the 36 move-record entry points, the 67 CALL_NATIVE targets and a routine index.

The script VM: all 52 opcodes, the decoder, the frame discipline, the two stack guards and the Q12 arithmetic with the exact rounding the ROM applies. CALL_NATIVE dispatches to an injected handler with no default. Imports nothing outside src; nothing imports it.

20 cases. The decisive one decodes all 63,748 blob bytes with the product decoder and requires it to close exactly on the end with all 1,290 branch targets on a boundary. The rest pin the table geometry and its terminator, every opcode's semantics on hand-built bytecode, the CALL/RETURN frame, both stack guards, and a smoke run of all 36 original entry points through the VM with a yielding native stub.

Transcribes the 103-entry table and the generator header. Takes the ROM path from --rom or YDIJ_ROM and hard-codes no drive letter. Refuses to emit unless the seed and cursor array pointers each occur exactly once in the whole ARM9 image -- which is the proof that only the roll and the seeder can touch the state.
The 103 table entries, the 217-channel header, the magic-division constants, the three master-seed call sites and the non-uniformity of the table.

The channel generator: the exact truncating remainder, the 217-channel seeding, and rng.next(channel) matching the interface the battle modules already take. A master seed of 0 is refused because it routes to the console clock. Imports nothing outside src.

12 cases. Pins the table and its three repeats and three gaps, checks the magic division against C truncating semantics across the int32 range, fixes the whole 217-channel state for master seed 0x14, proves channel 216 has period exactly 103, pins the six thresholds where the per-cycle rate is off by one, and drives battleStatus.tryApplyNegativeStatus with the real generator for a full cycle.

The eligibility rule and the match list. Walks title records 0..60 keeping those whose two schedule columns match the current slots and whose +0x10 requirement is at most the progress counter halved; entry mode 4 replaces the list with record 61. Also expands a team record into its three preset indices. Reads only the B1 catalogs; imports nothing outside src; nothing imports it.

9 cases. The load-bearing one proves the 4 x 8 schedule grid partitions all 61 reachable records exactly once with one empty cell; others pin the scan bound, the never-binding cap of 5, the `<=` progress gate at a record that needs a counter of 8, the unreachability of record 61, the entry-mode-4 override, and that all 152 teams together name each of the 456 presets exactly once.

The six-slot per-frame update: the four phases in the order the original visits them, the empty-slot skip that also escapes the counters, and the death path that still falls through into the counters. Adds no arithmetic -- the status tick is battleStatus.tickNegativeStatus. The four untraced routines the loop calls become named events carrying their ROM address.

14 cases pinning the phase order, ascending slot order, the empty-slot escape, the decrement-then-test DoT at 180 and 10, the `hp < 0` death test that spares an exact zero, the counters still ticking for a combatant that died this frame, the strict `>` threshold reachable only with no status, and the eight-entry table boundary cross-checked against battleActionSelection's move ladder.

The 27-state dispatcher: the suspend bit, the entry frame, the per-state period throttle including the zero-period case, and the entry counter of -255. Reports which handler would run rather than running one, because only four of the 27 bodies are traced. Imports nothing outside src.

14 cases pinning the table's 27 entries and both independent bounds on that count, the three states whose handlers are already-translated routines, the six inert `bx lr` states, the entry-then-period run pattern, period 0 meaning every frame, the suspend bit freezing the counter, and the cooldown gate cross-asserted against battleFrameLoop.

The 27 states' transitions, entry periods and reach, extracted mechanically from the handlers' bytes; plus the two handler bodies small enough to read whole (state 0 and state 11) implemented. Records that no state handler applies damage, and that the resolver hangs off script native 0x0211D71C.

10 cases pinning the graph shape, the hub-and-return structure, the inert states matching the four-byte handlers, the entry periods, both hand-read bodies, and the fact that the damage native is one the script blob actually calls.

The script native that lands an attack: the three-argument contract with a Q12 kind, the six-slot target walk and its four rejections in order, and which of the two parameter blocks reaches the damage resolver. Scope is the contract and the walk, not the whole 2,088-byte body.

The move-script layer: the three entry columns and where each is started, the six-argument frame for +0x3C, the Q12 conversion of the move record's signed bytes, the general argument-to-local mapping, and the built-in script at 0x0212F94E.

The strongest decodes the built-in script out of the committed blob with the product decoder and checks its prologue reads locals -5, -4, -3 -- arguments 2, 1, 0 -- exactly as the six-argument frame predicts. Others check all 1,755 non-null pointer values land on instruction boundaries and that the blob's negative locals are the contiguous run -3..-17.

The traced battle modules composed in the frame function's order. Runs the four states with translated bodies and the cooldown-to-action-gate chain; everywhere else it records a named seam with the ROM address whose body is missing and leaves the combatant untouched. Others pin the suspend bit freezing one slot's state counter but not its tick counters, state 11 releasing to the gate once its status is spent, and every untraced state naming its handler address without changing anything.

67 natives, 7,788 bytes, 3,014 call sites, with a shape classification and the field accesses each makes.

The catalog accessor plus the sixteen natives read line by line, each with its disassembly quoted. They cover 1,578 of the 3,014 call sites. A catalogued but unread address raises instead of answering.

14 cases driving every implemented native through a recording host: the chained and guarded getters, Q12 in both directions, the +1 before the shift, both compare-and-set routines, both guarded tail calls, the yield, and the sixteen-byte entry that forces kind 13 -- cross-asserted against battleActionApplication.

The nine-group candidate array and the two source words that fill it, with the 31-entry jump table transcribed. Resolves each entry's +0x48 cost through the B1 move catalog so the lists arrive in both shapes AI selection reads.

10 cases. The decisive one drives the real AI with buckets from this module and the original's channel-216 dice and gets twelve decisions, then replays them identically from the same seed. Others pin the array extent that fixes nine groups, the whole jump table, and that a code above 30 is dropped rather than filed.

The three launch slots at +0x78, the two wait-to-launch states read whole, the shared entry-frame abort of the three launch states, and the three interrupt predicates. States 4 and 5 are described and not implemented.

7 cases pinning the three-slot array from both ends, both wait states including the one notify that separates them, each launch state's own abort code, and both interrupt predicates. Cross-checked against the independently extracted state graph.
The twelve-object in-flight pool, its in-use bit, and the two gates that refuse a launch -- the +0x154 lock and the action-resource cost, both of which return zero and look identical to state 15.

9 cases pinning the pool size and its lowest-free discipline, the exhaustion arithmetic against three slots per combatant, the lock refusing before cost is even read, and the three-way join on +0x154 asserted against battleCandidateBuckets' own array extent.
The per-frame walk of the twelve in-flight objects, its two guards, and the kind dispatch whose kind 0 is the contact walk. Also carries the frame function's full eleven-loop order.

8 cases pinning the eleven-loop order with the in-flight walk between the two previously named phases, the kind-0-is-contact link, both update guards, and the +0xE4 / +0x94 offsets asserted equal to the ones battleActionApplication reads.

How a battle ends and who is judged to have won. Two end conditions (a wiped team; the clock passing 7200 frames, tested with ble so frame 7200 still plays), the eight-step 900-frame tier, the judge (more standing wins; on a tie, the greater float32 sum of HP/maxHP; exactly level is verdict 5), the demotion of 5 to 3, the per-round win-flag array with its cursor, the mode-3 tally capped at 9999, and the OVL8 payout gate that requires every round of the tournament. No invented tiebreak and no invented outcome.

14 cases. The clock divisor 900 is re-derived from the magic 0x91A2B3C5 over 20,000 values inside the test rather than asserted as a constant. Other cases pin the strictly-greater time test, the no-early-exit double judge, that a type-2 battle inverts the test rather than the verdict, that the level demotion cannot change any win flag, and that one lost round takes the whole payout.

The VS5 Auto Battle scene on the single Championship Pixi stage. Draws the five bands with Graphics only: a clock bar with one pip per 900-frame tier, two HUD rows, a procedural neutral arena, and a result plate. No pointer handling at all, because the battle takes no input.

14 cases. The band geometry, the exact 9:16 reference, that the field band is exactly 3:2, that every HUD field names a traced site, that no contract value is loadable as a path, and that the module carries no accuracy or damage-number identifier.

10 cases against a recording Graphics stub: the frame centres and never stretches, the bands tile with no gap, cyberspace gets no common ring, the scene registers exactly one ticker and one resize observer and removes both, the battle stops itself and is still drawn, and the three battle screens route as the ROM's own screen names do.
Transcribes the creature stat curve and the species stat index. Refuses to emit if curve columns 1..6 stop being identical, if column 0 stops ascending, or if any species indexes outside the 27 rows.

228 species records. Only +0x30 is transcribed, because it is the only field with a traced read site on the battle path: it indexes the stat curve for HP.

Turns an opponent preset into the creature record a combatant carries at +0x10. The preset-to-creature mapping was derived by emulating the decoded instruction stream rather than read by eye. Every stat is a curve row read back; nothing is computed.

9 cases. All 456 presets build; the 27 that name the absent species are refused; the single record carrying a -1 level is proven unreachable rather than clamped; two presets of one species get the same HP and different resource.

The AI cascade applies three different liveness rules: group 1 skips HP exactly 0, group 3 applies no HP test at all, group 5 requires HP > 0. battleContactTargeting separately requires HP > 0, so a negative-HP combatant can be targeted and then rejected at contact. All four rules are in the ROM.

OVL19 0x021300D4 maps action id to the positive effect code it applies (ids 0-9 -> 0, then pairs 10/11 -> 1 up to 22/23 -> 7). Group 6 uses it to decline an action whose effect the combatant already carries; this is the duplicate-effect logic Stage 6 saw while auditing Sense.

Stage 4 B07/B08 and the Cursor handoff both treated TP as an invention risk. It is not: OVL19 0x0211C244 charges action +0x48 against stats +0x54 with a refuse-if-insufficient guard. The shared unknown register should be corrected.
The move table's record count is in the ROM, not inferred: OVL19 0x02113DFC is `cmp r2,#0x254 / blo`, so the scan walks records 0..595 at the 0x68 stride the MLA at 0x02113DCC forms.
The opponent-team table's three index columns flatten to exactly 0..455 in order, one per battle-preset record. That is a bijection, so 152 teams and 456 presets confirm each other.
The message-id space is contiguous across three of these tables: opponent teams hold 0x323..0x3BA and 0x3BB..0x452, and the eligibility table's id column takes the next id 0x453 and runs to 0x47F.
Species ids 2..19 own no move record at all; 206 of the 224 ids own between 1 and 30. Species 1 owns 30, more than the eight the OVL19 scan will collect.
The title table's +0x08 column is a permutation of 0..61 rather than the identity: records 12 and 51 swap. It is still a bijection, so the count of 62 holds.
Record 61 of the title table is the only record in it with a zero +0x24. The OVL8 no-reward special case is now pinned from the data instead of asserted.

The battle script VM is generic engine code in ARM9, not battle code: the dispatch is at 0x020549D4 and the handlers at 0x02054A5C..0x0205568C, with the compiler's own 'script.cpp' assert strings sitting immediately after the 52-entry table at 0x020BDEAC. The table's own terminator is what fixes the opcode count.

It is a stack machine over one flat 96-slot array, using C++ pointer-to-member dispatch with an 8-byte stride. init fakes a caller frame with a zero return address, which is why RETURN's stop condition is a restored pc of exactly 0.

The scripts are Q12 fixed-point throughout: the whole integer arithmetic family (0x0B..0x11) is unused across all 23,121 instructions, while 0x13..0x19 are common. 0x15 rounds with +0x800, 0x16 uses the hardware divider on a value shifted left 32, and 0x18/0x19 step by 0x1000.
OVL19 0x021204A0..0x0212FDA4 is one contiguous 63,748-byte bytecode blob, 23,121 instructions, entered at 36 addresses taken from move-record fields +0x1C, +0x28 and +0x3C.

The original's stack-overflow assert is only a print: CALL and CALL_NATIVE check sp against 0x5E and 0x60, and on failure the push still runs off the slot array into sp and frameBase. The product VM raises there instead of reproducing the overrun.

The channel RNG is not a stream. The roll reads seed[channel] and never writes it, so each channel is one fixed cycle of period 103: critical hits and status procs repeat every 103 rolls on their channel.

The 103-entry table is NOT a permutation of 0..102. It holds 100 distinct values: 0, 50 and 99 each appear twice and 46, 100 and 102 never appear. A roll is therefore not uniform, and `roll < T` does not always hit exactly T times per cycle.

At the one master seed the ROM hard-codes (0x14 at OVL9 0x021775DC), channel 216's per-cycle hit count is exactly T for every threshold up to 15 -- which covers the critical thresholds 2, 3, 5 and 7 -- and off by exactly one at six thresholds above it. The earlier estimate of 1.9%-6.8% for the critical thresholds is confirmed exactly, not approximately.
The seed array 0x02104D20 and the cursor array 0x02105084 are adjacent, 217 words apart, and each pointer appears exactly once in the whole ARM9 image, inside the header at 0x020BD230.

The ROM's `% 103` is a signed truncating remainder implemented as smull by 0x13E22CBD then asr #3 plus the sign bit. It matches C semantics across the whole int32 range, so a negative operand yields a negative remainder with no correction.

The title-event table's +0x14 and +0x18 are a schedule key. Across the 4 x 8 grid the filter compares against, all 61 reachable records appear exactly once -- no record in two cells, none left over -- and one cell (slot A 3, slot B 4) holds no match.
The match list is capped at 5 by OVL10 0x0210EC2C, but the cap never binds: the busiest schedule cell holds four.

Not one of the 61 records the filter can reach has a zero payout. Record 61, the table's only zero, is exactly the one the filter cannot reach and the one entry mode 4 forces -- so B1's zero-payout finding and OVL8's no-reward behavior are one fact.

The word that forces the record-61 list is written at exactly one address in the whole ROM, OVL10 0x0210B498, guarded by `cmp r0,#4` on the global context +0xA8. Two independent whole-image scans agree there is no other writer.

OVL10 0x0211057C..0x02110594 loads a team record's +0x00/+0x04/+0x08 at stride 0x14 and multiplies each by 0x44 into the preset table. That is the ROM confirming B1's corrected team base 0x020ED2D8 from the consuming side.
-1 is the empty sentinel for both a team index (OVL10 0x02110560) and a preset slot inside a team (0x021105CC).

The per-frame update is OVL19 0x0210D6E4, 137 instructions over six slots, and its phase order is: negative status, then a threshold check reachable only when there is no status, then a gated timer, then the +0x24 and +0x28 counters.

An empty roster slot branches straight to the loop increment, so it escapes the counters as well as everything else. A combatant that dies during the status phase does NOT: the death handler branches into the timer phase and falls through into both counters.

The death test is `bge`, so a damage-over-time tick that lands a combatant exactly on 0 HP leaves it alive with its status still running. Only a negative result kills, and the negative is stored back as 0.

The threshold table at OVL19 0x0212FE74 is eight u16 entries, [100, 100, 100, 9999, 50, 9999, 50, 9999]; it is eight because battleActionSelection's move-ladder table starts sixteen bytes later at 0x0212FE84, whose first row is 68, 89.

The per-frame battle function is OVL19 0x0210D33C and it runs two six-slot loops in order: state dispatch at 0x0210D644, then the status and counter tick at 0x0210D6E4. Both ascending, both skipping an empty slot.

The battle state machine has 27 states in a table at OVL19 0x0213040C with stride 8 -- the same C++ pointer-to-member form the script VM's opcode table uses. Two independent bounds agree: the 28th entry would not be an OVL19 address, and the literal state codes any of the 70 `bl 0x02114984` sites passes are 0, 1, 3..16 and 23.

A state handler runs on the frame it is entered and after that only when the state's frame counter at +0x16C divides exactly by its period at +0x170. A period of 0 reaches the divide's zero path at ARM9 0x0202B750 and leaves the remainder at 0, so period 0 means EVERY frame, not never.
Bit 1 of the u16 at combatant +0x9A suspends the state machine for that combatant: no handler runs and the state counter does not advance either.
State 2, AI action selection, is never set by a literal `mov r1` anywhere in OVL19. It is only reached from inside the machine.
States 17 through 22 are six consecutive `bx lr` stubs at 0x021170B8..0x021170CC -- real table entries that do nothing, and none is a code the ROM sets.

0x0211479C, the frame loop's timer call-out, is NOT 'this combatant may act'. It clears +0x160 and +0x164 plus two per-combatant globals and returns the HP compare. An earlier working guess in this lane said otherwise and was wrong.

The battle state machine's graph: state 1 (the action gate) fans out to 3, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13; state 2 (AI selection) fans out to 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; the 4/5/6/7 group leads into 14/15/16 and all three return to 1; state 11 waits out a status then returns to 1 or drops to 0 when dead; state 0 arms a 60-frame period and does nothing else.

No state handler applies damage or walks contact. The damage resolver's three call sites are one inside the contact walk and two inside 0x0211D71C, a battle-script CALL_NATIVE target. The state machine schedules and the move's bytecode executes.
OVL9 is 487 KiB -- 45% of all overlay space -- and it is the character and graphics resource manager, not game logic. That materially shrinks the remaining reverse-engineering surface.

The game-logic overlays are OVL0 (hunting, 126 KiB), OVL8 (rewards, 18 KiB), OVL10 (match selection, 40 KiB), OVL18 (raising and schedule, 118 KiB) and OVL19 (battle, 154 KiB). Everything else is a screen, the resource manager, or a stub.

An attack lands through OVL19 0x0211D71C, a script CALL_NATIVE taking three arguments: the action object, an optional parameter block, and a Q12 number truncated with `asr #0xc`. The attacker is action +0xE4.

That native walks the same six-slot roster the frame loop does, ascending, and rejects a target on four counts in order: empty slot, the attacker itself, matching +0x54 on both sides, and the attacker having a non-zero +0x94 while the target's is zero. It returns how many survived.
An attacker whose status at +0x158 is exactly 5 skips the same-side rejection outright, so its own side becomes targetable. Self is still rejected first.
The damage resolver's parameter block is three words: either [action +0x00] + 0x28 when script argument 1 is zero, or argument1 + 0x24 otherwise.

The move record is [combatant +0x20] and [action +0x20]. Its +0x1C and +0x28 columns start scripts on the combatant's VM at +0xEC; its +0x3C column starts one on the action object's own VM at +0x2A0. A move therefore runs more than one script, on more than one VM.

Whatever the argument count, a script reads init argument k as local -(k+3) -- init pushes the array in reverse and then two zeros, so the mapping is independent of N. Across the whole blob the negative locals used are exactly the contiguous run -3 to -17 and nothing reads -1 or -2, which is what that predicts.

The 445-byte run at 0x0212F94E that B2's reachability walk could not account for is a built-in action script: OVL19 0x0211DD14 loads it as a literal and starts it with the same six-argument frame a move's own +0x3C script gets. It is 161 instructions and reserves 8 locals.

Move-record bytes +0x40 and +0x41 are constant zero across all 596 records, so two of the six script arguments are base words unchanged in every retail move. +0x43 is -1 on 585 records and 0..4 on eleven, so the third Q12 argument is -1.0 for almost every move.

The traced battle modules do compose. A six-slot session runs the frame function's two loops in order and carries every slot from a spent cooldown through the action gate; the chain breaks in exactly one place, at the AI's candidate buckets.

Composition found two defects that per-module cases could not: battleFrameLoop's strict field check blocked ticking a combatant that also carries state-machine fields, and a state handler must see the frame counter BEFORE the dispatcher's increment or an entry frame is not recognised as one.
Only 4 of the 27 battle states have runnable bodies today: 0, 1, 3 and 11. Eight more are inert stubs, leaving seventeen with a profile but no translation.
The 67 script natives are 7,788 bytes but lopsided: four routines are half of that and the other sixty-three average sixty bytes. By shape: 41 compound, 10 getters, 10 setters, 5 trivial, 1 yield.

OVL19 0x0211D70C is sixteen bytes -- `ldr ip,=0x0211D740 / mov r1,#0xd / bx ip` -- a tail call into the action-application body with the kind forced to 13. The kind-13 branch battleActionApplication found special is this entry, and the blob calls it 56 times.

0x0211CEC4 and 0x0211CEFC are two separate routines that both compare-and-set +0x154: they write only into an empty slot and return whether they wrote. A caller cannot treat either as a plain assignment.
0x0211D2BC reads a u8 at +0x58, adds one, and returns it in Q12 -- so the value the scripts see is one-based, not the stored byte.
0x0211D2E0 shifts its callee's result left by 20, not 12, so not every native that returns a scaled number is returning Q12.

The candidate array is nine groups of twelve bytes -- two word entries at +0xE8 and a byte count at +0xF0 -- and its extent is what fixes the count: 0xE8 + 9*12 is exactly 0x154, where the next field begins.

Only two entries are ever filed into that whole array, both from stats +0x12C and +0x130. A source code above 30 falls to group 0 and is dropped, and group 0 is never filed. Most buckets are empty in most frames, and the AI treats that as normal.

A bucket entry is an action id: the affordability scan indexes the move table with it at 0x02114500, and the same +0x12C field is used that way at 0x02111344. The bucket group index and the AI's state code are the same number.

The original files a bucket entry with no bound check and would write past a group's two words into the next group's count byte. Two sources cannot reach it, but the overrun is real and is refused rather than reproduced.

State 1 commits an action object taken from a pool at combatant +0x58, not the action the AI names. It releases a previous claim only when the object differs, stores the claim at +0x5C, and then rebuilds the cooldown.

The action cooldown is 90 - 2*speed from stats +0x8C, reduced to 80% when +0x160 is exactly 3. A speed of 45 yields zero and anything higher goes negative, and since the gate is `<= 0` and the tick is `subgt`, such a combatant is permanently ready.

+0x160 is one field read three ways that now agree: the frame loop gates its timer on it being non-zero, the cooldown takes 80% when it is 3, and AI group 6 declines an action whose effect is already carried. 0x0211479C clears +0x160 and +0x164 together, so that timer is the effect's duration.
With the pool supplied, the composed battle session runs a self-sustaining loop with zero seams: choose, commit, cool down, choose again -- and the same master seed replays it exactly.

A combatant can have at most three actions in flight: +0x78, +0x7C and +0x80. State 15 allocates into the first free one and the predicate at 0x02114464 gates states 6 and 7 on one being free, so a fourth action waits.

States 6 and 7 are the same routine but for one line -- a free slot advances to 15 or 16 respectively, otherwise the combatant waits out its cooldown and re-enters the action gate. Only state 7 notifies on its entry frame.
States 14, 15 and 16 abort back to state 1 on their entry frame when +0x180 is negative, and on +0x17C being 8..11 for 14 and 15 but 12 for 16. Nothing is tested after the entry frame.
0x02114490 answers yes when +0x17C is 18..21 and otherwise returns bit 1 of +0x9A -- the same suspend bit the state dispatcher reads, so a suspended combatant reads as interrupted here too.

States 4 and 5 are approach geometry: an angle tested against 0x4000 and 0xC000, the quarter and three-quarter turns of a 16-bit angle, offsetting a target by 0x10000 before a DS math call at 0x02003098.

A launch raises a notify equal to the move record's own +0x10 plus eight -- 8, 9, 10 or 11. Every one of the 596 records holds a value inside 0..3, so every launch in the game raises one of the four, and B1's catalogued field is confirmed from its consuming side.

The launch's two failure paths are literally the same three lines at 0x02116D40 and 0x02116E00: clear bit 0 of the new object, zero the slot, and go back to state 1. A null allocation is different again -- the slot is already clear and the handler simply returns with no transition.
A successful launch adds 120 to the signed halfword at combatant +0x1C, read with ldrsh and stored with strh, so it wraps at 16 bits.
A battle shares twelve in-flight objects at globalCtx + 0x47948, and bit 0 of each object's first word is its in-use flag. A combatant holds at most three, so four of the six can exhaust the pool.

A launch is refused by the action-resource charge at 0x0211C144 for one of two reasons -- a non-zero +0x154, tested before cost is even read, or a cost above the balance -- and state 15 cannot tell them apart. Either way the object goes back to the pool and the combatant returns to state 1.
+0x154 is one field three independent traces landed on: the two script natives compare-and-set it, the launch charge refuses on it, and the nine-group candidate array ends exactly there.

The frame function runs eleven loops, not two. In address order with bounds: 0x0210D3C0/6, 0x0210D490/12, 0x0210D4F8/6, 0x0210D590/6, 0x0210D624/2, 0x0210D644/6 state dispatch, 0x0210D694/12 in-flight update, 0x0210D6E4/6 status and counters, 0x0210D9A8/6, 0x0210DC58/6, 0x0210DD18/2.
Damage reaches the roster through the in-flight update: 0x0211CC7C dispatches on the object's +0x04 kind and kind 0 is the contact walk at 0x0211C714, which calls the resolver at 0x0211C92C.

An in-flight object's update refuses twice first: no owner at +0xE4 does nothing, and an owner whose +0x94 names a different object does nothing. Only a null lock or one naming this object lets it run.

An in-flight object and the 'action object' a move script operates on are the same thing: both read their owner at +0xE4, and battleActionApplication's fourth target rejection reads the owner's +0x94 lock from the other side.

entries20260902.item: Nobody takes damage yet, and the reason is a composition gap not a missing formula
entries20260902.detail: battleSession runs dispatch, the action gate, AI selection, the commit and the cooldown, and stops there. Damage comes from the in-flight walk to the contact walk to the resolver, and those three modules exist and are tested but the session does not call them. Over 300 frames a real match emits 1200 gates, 1200 choices, 12 commits and 8 releases, and no seams: the twelve-object pool fills and is never freed because the in-flight phase that would run an object to completion is not wired in. That is the next composition step.

entries20260902.item: Damage is wired end to end, and the last blocker is a bucket mismatch with a traced answer
entries20260902.detail: battleSession now runs the in-flight phase and applies HP; a session test drives six slots to real damage with no seam left. A live match still does no damage, and the reason is now traced rather than guessed: selectBattleAiAction reads its three buckets from combatant +0xE4/+0xE5/+0xE6, which the creature loader at OVL19 0x02113D88 writes (0x02113E9C, 0x02113ED0, 0x02113F08) while classifying the up-to-eight moves it scanned out of the 596-record table for that species. The session instead passes buildCandidateBuckets' nine groups, which live at +0xE8 + group*12 and feed the TARGETED cascade, not these three. So the session is right about its "targeted" argument and wrong about its "candidateBuckets" one. Closing it needs the classification rule at 0x02113E60..0x02113F08, which is the next read.

entries20260902.item: The action element system is traced
entries20260902.detail: A move record's +0x58 selects which of six defender levels resists it: selector 0 or above 5 uses creature +0x88, and 1..5 use +0x94, +0x98, +0x9C, +0xA0, +0xA4. Each branch is raised one curve step by its own buff code (2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 7) on the defender's +0x160. Those offsets are exactly the level fields the creature builder writes from preset +0x1C..+0x38.

entries20260902.item: Codex was right on three counts and they are fixed
entries20260902.detail: The Battle screen shipped three of the five bands the contract declares, the CSS locked only the field, and the contract note over-claimed the band layout as the original second screen. All three corrected and verified in a browser at 375x812: shell ratio 0.5625, bands measured at exactly 5, 10, 37.5, 28 and 19.5 per cent, field ratio 1.500. entries20260902.item: The AI bucket question is answered, and the buckets are not the nine groups
entries20260902.detail: OVL19 0x02113E5C classifies the creature move list into three buckets by the move record +0x50: kind 0 fills the array at +0xC0 counted at +0xE4, kind 1 with +0x0C == 1 fills +0xCC counted at +0xE5, kind 1 with +0x0C == 2 fills +0xD8 counted at +0xE6, three each. The AI reads those counts at 0x02115B28, 0x02115A80 and 0x02115AD4, so bucket 4 is +0xE4, bucket 5 is +0xE5 and bucket 6 is +0xE6. Contact kinds 2 and 3 are never bucketed, so every attack comes through the targeted cascade, which takes the nine groups the session already passes. The session was right about targeted and its candidateBuckets argument is a separate, smaller job.

entries20260902.item: Two inputs the session never supplied, one fixed and one open
entries20260902.detail: targeted.roster is now wired: the cascade scans it for a target and without it group 1 and group 3 always reported NO_TARGET. sessionScalarIndex is still open: it indexes the reserve percentages, 0 yields a reserve of 0, and the gate is cost < reserve, so at 0 no action is ever affordable. Where the original sets it is not traced. With a roster and a non-zero scalar the AI commits, verified over 3000 draws.

entries20260902.item: A power question worth answering before trusting any damage number
entries20260902.detail: Only 30 of the 596 move records carry a contact kind, and their +0x4A power holds just two distinct values, 0 and 15. The resolver reads power from action +0x20 then +0x4A, and this lane has assumed that record is the move record. Either most contact moves really do zero damage, or +0x4A is not the field the resolver ends up reading. That is the next thing to settle, because every damage number depends on it.

entries20260902.item: The power field is correct; the damage PATH was the wrong one
entries20260902.detail: Proof that action +0x20 is a move-table record: 0x0211C188 compares its +0x28 against the literal 0x02120D8A, and 262 of the 596 records carry exactly that pointer. So +0x4A really is the power the resolver multiplies by. What was wrong is which moves reach it. The jump table at 0x021149E8 reads pc as 0x021149F0, so kind 0 and kind 1 go to the curve-and-power path at 0x02114A00, kind 2 goes to 0x02115504 and kind 3 returns. The table divides as 205 kind-0 moves (powers 0, 100, 300), 361 kind-1 (27 distinct powers, 30 to 600), 27 kind-2 (0 or 15) and 3 kind-3 (0). The contact walk proceeds only for kinds 2 and 3, exactly the kinds the switch sends elsewhere.

entries20260902.item: The ordinary attack is resolved by a script native, not by the contact walk
entries20260902.detail: The resolver has three callers. One is the contact walk at 0x0211C92C; the other two, 0x0211D9E0 and 0x0211D9FC, are both inside the 2,124-byte script native at 0x0211D71C. That native was earlier called presentation plumbing because every store in it lands in the handle arrays, which was true and incomplete: it also calls the resolver twice. So a normal attack runs as a MOVE SCRIPT on the VM, which calls that native, which resolves the damage. battleInFlight said the chain closed at the contact walk; that claim is now corrected in the file and a test holds the correction.

entries20260902.item: The AI now commits real attack moves, and the two reasons it never did are both traced
entries20260902.detail: First, the reserve scalar is the clock tier. 0x021159F0 reads ctx +0xE9C, the eight-step tier battleOutcome advances every 900 frames, and indexes the percent table at 0x0212FFF4 with it. Two of the three profiles reserve nothing at tier 0, so the original opens a match passive and grows willing as the clock runs out. The session was passing a per-combatant field that defaulted to 0. Second, the ladder buckets are the creature move list classified by kind at 0x02113E5C, not the nine candidate groups from the two source codes; the nine belong to the targeted cascade, which the session was already passing correctly. With both fixed a real match commits move 98 for its species, a kind-0 move of power 100 and cost 0, out of bucket 4 which carries no cost gate. That is why a match is not silent at tier 0 even when the reserve is zero.

entries20260902.item: Running move scripts works, and it needs an Owner decision about what ships
entries20260902.detail: The VM executes the cartridge bytecode. Feeding a real move record entry point into battleScriptVm runs it and dispatches real natives: 15, 6 and 20 distinct ones from the three pointers a record carries. Reachability was measured first, and there is no small subset: decoding from all 36 move entry points and following every in-range target visits 22,032 of the segment 23,121 instructions and touches 63,747 of its 63,748 bytes. So making move scripts run means carrying the whole 63,748-byte segment, about 86 KB as base64. The migration firewall payload test matches on file extensions and a .json would pass it, but the test is titled no ROM, Nitro, decoded, or forensic payload, and the intent plainly covers this. The extractor is written and proven; nothing has been placed in src/.

entries20260902.item: A move record names three scripts, and all three point into the segment
entries20260902.detail: pointer1C has 3 distinct values across 595 records, pointer28 has 31 across 565, pointer3C has 2 across 595, and every one of them is a move-record entry point. The launch initialiser at 0x0211C198 rewrites two of them in place before use: a record whose +0x0C is 1 and whose +0x28 is 0x02124D82 gets +0x28 set to 0x02120D8A, and a record whose +0x1C is 0x02120674 and whose +0x28 is 0x02120D8A gets +0x1C set to 0x02120754. It also refuses the launch outright when 0x0210FA28 says anyone is engaged.

entries20260902.item: What still blocks real damage after the scripts run
entries20260902.detail: The scripts run on an all-zero action object, so their conditionals take the wrong branches and none of the three reached 0x0211D71C, the native that calls the resolver. Two of the three ended in RUN_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED and one in DIV_FX_BY_ZERO_UNTRACED, both consistent with missing object state rather than with a wrong decode. The remaining work is modelling the action object the scripts read, not more tracing of the VM.

entries20260902.item: The script segment was already in the tree, and the decision ratified it rather than authorizing it
entries20260902.detail: The Owner was asked whether to carry the 63,748-byte OVL19 script segment and said yes. It then turned out battle-scripts.r1.json has carried it in blob.base64 since the B2 pass, byte for byte identical, sha e089685d. A second copy was written and has been deleted; battleMoveScriptRun reads the one that was always there. Two things follow. The decision stands and is now recorded. And the migration firewall payload test matches on file extensions, so it never saw this: a case has been added that names the one authorized segment and fails if a second appears.

entries20260902.item: Move scripts now execute, and the next step is a short list of small natives
entries20260902.detail: A real attack move record runs on the VM through its +0x3C column with the traced six-argument frame and dispatches 20 distinct natives. It does not yet reach 0x0211D71C because every native returns 0 from a stub, so the script spins instead of progressing. The hot ones are small: 0x0211D3A8 at 32 bytes called 1,083 times, 0x0211D54C at 84, 0x0211D3C8 at 80, 0x0211D1E0 at 28, three 24-byte ones, 0x0211D2E0 at 56, and 0x0211E28C at 16 bytes with zero arguments and yields true, which is the per-frame yield the spin is waiting on. Implementing that handful is what turns a spinning script into a running one.

entries20260902.item: Move scripts now run to completion, and the blocker was the yield
entries20260902.detail: 0x0211E28C is sixteen bytes: bl 0x02054A24 and return 0, the per-frame yield. A caller stub that merely returned 0 for it kept the script inside one resume until the budget ran out, which read like a decode fault and was not one. Routing natives to battleScriptNatives, whose implementation of that address actually yields, turned a spinning script into one that executes 280 instructions and ends cleanly. Sweeping every distinct script address in the move table: 36 run, 9 finish clean, 27 still error on an unread native, and 1 reaches 0x0211D71C, the routine that calls the damage resolver.

entries20260902.item: Nine natives read, and the ranked list of what is left
entries20260902.detail: 0x02054A34 is the argument read, 0x02054A24 the yield. 0x02047C48 returns 1 when the object +0x7C is zero and 0 otherwise, an is-it-finished poll a single attack script runs 1,083 times. Three 24-byte getters read a three-word vector through +0x2C at +0x00, +0x04 and +0x08, and 0x0211D54C writes the second and third of them, so +0x2C is a position block written and read by the same script. Seven of the nine were already implemented from an earlier pass; the two that were not are now. What blocks the remaining 27 scripts, ranked by how many want it: 0x0211E2C4 wanted by 25 of 36 at 20 bytes and one argument, then 0x0211D238 and 0x0211D298 by 18 each, 0x0211D418 by 17, 0x0211DF68 by 13.

entries20260902.item: The move-script stage went from 9 of 36 scripts running to 26, and the blocker was never the natives
entries20260902.detail: Two diagnostics did the work. Stubbing the animation natives with plausible values changed nothing, which ruled them out. Reading the calls that preceded a failure showed every accessor receiving argument zero, which pointed at the frame rather than the routine. battleMoveScript had recorded the +0x1C and +0x28 argument counts as null because they had never been traced, so the runner passed no arguments at all: every arg(0) was zero, the accessor natives returned zero and the scripts divided by zero. It read like a decode fault for two sittings and was an empty frame. 0x0211C51C passes 8 and 0x0211CABC passes 14, both now recorded slot by slot.

entries20260902.item: Twelve more natives, including the DS square root and the trig table
entries20260902.detail: 0x0211E2C4 is the DS hardware square root: SQRTCNT at 0x040002B0 in 64-bit mode, and a value at or below zero returns zero without touching it. 0x0211E2D8 and 0x0211E304 read a 4,096-entry table of signed halfword pairs at 0x02099D6C; comparing the whole table against round(4096 * sin) and its cosine gave zero mismatches across all 4,096 rows and both columns, so the closed form is the table and 16 KB of it did not need carrying. 0x0211E29C rolls channel 216, the same cycle the crit and variance rolls use, and takes the remainder modulo a Q12 argument.

entries20260902.item: What actually blocks the last ten scripts
entries20260902.detail: Not natives and not the decode. The scripts now run far enough to read the in-flight object graph: 0x0211D050 fetches the action at +0xE8, the three getters chain through +0x2C to a position block, and the host memory those reads land in is empty. Seeding a crude graph by hand moved one more script from errored to clean, which is the proof. The next read is the launch initialiser at 0x0211C098, which is what sets those fields up.

entries20260902.item: The launch position is traced, and every remaining thread converges on one routine
entries20260902.detail: OVL19 0x0211C098 fetches the current animation cell through 0x02047E58, reads the three-word position block at +0x2C, and places the new object at the owner position plus half of x0 plus x1 shifted twelve, the same for y, with z untouched and the rounding toward zero. That block is the same one the three script getters at 0x0211CE7C, 0x0211CE94 and 0x0211CEAC read and 0x0211D418 writes, so four routines and the launch all share it. The consequence for the stage: the launch position and the three unread animation natives are not two dependencies but one. 0x02047E58 reads the creature loaded sprite data, which is the art lane asset rather than anything a battle table holds, so the cell box is modelled as an input and not derived.

entries20260902.item: A match deals damage end to end for the first time
entries20260902.detail: Player 760 down to -62, -18 and -8, opponent untouched, ended at frame 7201 on TIME_UP with verdict TEAM_ONE_AHEAD. The chain is AI selection, the move buckets, the move script running the cartridge bytecode on the traced VM, the attack native 0x0211D71C, the resolver at 0x021149A8 and applyBattleHp. The attack runs on the +0x28 column and not +0x3C. Three composition bugs surfaced only by running it: a catalog key of battle-moves where the catalog says moves, with a try/catch swallowing the miss so every action carried a null move; speciesId never reaching the combatant so all six bucketed as species 0; and the side field at +0x54 never being set so every target was refused as SAME_SIDE. None was a bad reading of the ROM; all three were wiring.

entries20260902.item: The product creatures cannot attack, and that is a decision not a bug
entries20260902.detail: Greyshade Cat and the other two have no ROM species id, so buildMoveBucketsForSpecies gives them species 0 and they commit a move that never reaches the attack. In the run above the opponent took no damage at all for exactly this reason. They need declared move lists the way they already have declared levels, and which moves they carry is an Owner call rather than something the cartridge can answer.

entries20260902.item: A player write-up corroborates the schedule pair, and answers nothing else
entries20260902.detail: The Owner supplied a Bahamut forum post about the original. Treated as a SECONDARY source throughout: nothing traced was changed and no number was taken from it. One thing lines up usefully. The post describes the calendar as four seasons a year, eight days a season, and battleMatchSelection dumped the schedule moduli as 4 and 8 weeks ago, so slotA reads as the season and slotB as the day. That makes the runtime default legible as season 2 day 3 while leaving it product-authored, because where a fresh save actually starts is still untraced. Two smaller notes: the post lists the trainable stats as HP, TP, attack, defence, one unclear term and agility, which is six and matches the six defender branches at 0x02114A8C, and it calls the action resource TP, which is a player-facing name for the field this lane traced as charged by the action cost at 0x0211C244. Neither is being used to rename anything. What the post does NOT cover, and I looked for it specifically: whether the player controls a fight or it runs itself, what the battle screen shows, and any time limit. So the VS5 Auto Battle reading still rests on the trace alone -- no traced site reads player input between the start of a match and its verdict.
